passage: You asked how we handle the job question, so I'll tell you. I'm Ramesh, and Anjali and I have been together two years. Last month I got an interview in Hyderabad. Anjali is here, in Pune, on her third year. We could not decide anything, only worry. So one evening we did something different. We wrote three futures on a page. One: I get the job and move. Two: Anjali gets an offer somewhere else. Three: both stay put. For each we asked what we would do for the first year. Not promises, just options: visits every six weeks, a review call after each result. We agreed to look at the page again in March. I thought it would be dry. It felt kind, honestly. Every future had a way through, and none needed a promise tonight.

qa.a: They agreed to look at the page again in March.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the pair add, and why?
qa.a: They could learn about the real costs and timelines of each city, because a plan for a future is stronger with facts than with guesses.

qa.q: How might Anjali see the page of three futures?

I'm Lokesh, Shalini's younger brother, and our flat has thin walls. Last Sunday I heard her and Karthik on a long call, and it was the calmest serious talk I've ever heard two people have.
Shalini had a list. 'Option one: I get the Hyderabad job, you finish your master's in Chennai, we visit monthly for a year. Option two: you get placed in Hyderabad too. Option three: neither of us gets Hyderabad. Then what?'
Karthik said something I couldn't hear. Shalini laughed and said, 'No, I'm not asking you to promise anything. I just want us to have thought about it before it happens.'
They went through each option: what it would cost, who would move, what would feel unfair. At the end she said, 'Let's look at this again in June, after results.'
I can't know what she felt, but she hummed while making dinner.

qa.q: When did Shalini suggest looking at the plan again?
What does Shalini's 'I'm not asking you to promise anything' suggest about her?
qa.a: She seems calm and thoughtful, wanting to feel prepared rather than anxious, without pressuring Karthik into a promise.

qa.q: What else could the couple add to their options?
qa.a: A note on what each would need to feel supported in each option, so the June talk covers feelings as well as practical steps.

qa.q: How does the call sound to Lokesh through the thin walls?
qa.a: To Lokesh it sounds unusually calm for a serious talk, and Shalini humming afterward suggests it went well.

grounding: Shows a couple talking through several possible futures after graduation and agreeing to revisit the plan in June without forcing a promise.

subtype: Approach: contingency planning for career moves [Thinking]
passage:
January, a Saturday. Tarun, in his last semester in Jaipur, gets an interview call from a firm in Singapore. His partner Leena is doing her MBA in Ahmedabad for another year. That night on the phone, instead of panicking, they list what could happen: he gets it; he doesn't; he gets something in India instead. For each one they ask: what would we do, and what would we need from each other?
February, a Tuesday. Tarun's friend Akash asks whether Leena made him promise to turn it down. 'No promises,' Tarun says. 'We just agreed that if it comes, we try one year, and we talk again in August.'
April, a Friday. The offer arrives. Tarun calls Leena first. They don't argue about whether. They open the note from January and talk about when.

qa.q: Where is Leena doing her MBA?
How might Tarun have been feeling when the offer arrived in April?
qa.a: He was likely excited but steady rather than panicked, since they had already thought through this possibility.

qa.q: What else could Tarun and Leena plan before he leaves?
qa.a: Set their call routine and put the August check-in in the calendar, so 'try one year' has a clear shape.

qa.q: What is Akash's view of the plan in February?
qa.a: Akash expects Leena to have demanded a promise and seems surprised to hear there are none, just an agreed time to talk again.

grounding: Shows a couple listing possible outcomes of a job interview abroad, agreeing to try a year and revisit in August, without forcing a promise.
